Potato Late Blight Research Series 
Trichoderma asperellum Biocontrol & Ridomil Application Studies 
KALRO Tigoni, Kenya | 2019-2021 
 
Document Purpose & RAG Usage Guide 
This document is structured for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) applications. Each 
section is self-contained with clearly labelled context, enabling accurate retrieval and contextual 
injection when users pose questions about potato late blight management, biocontrol agents, 
fungicide use, pesticide residues, and related agronomic economics in sub-Saharan Africa. 
 
How this document is organized for RAG: 
• Each paper is treated as an independent knowledge node with unique metadata. 
• Key findings are stated as direct, queryable facts. 
• Numerical data (yields, concentrations, MRR%, residue levels) are retained precisely for 
factual retrieval. 
• Cross-paper relationships are explicitly noted to support multi-document reasoning. 
• Terminology is consistent and aligned with the source papers.

Shared Research Context 
Study Location 
All field experiments were conducted at Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research 
Organization (KALRO) Tigoni, Limuru, Kiambu County, Kenya. Site coordinates: latitude 10 
degrees 9 minutes 22 seconds south, longitude 36 degrees 4 minutes 72 seconds east. 
Altitude: 2,300 m above sea level. Annual rainfall: 1,800 mm. Temperature range: 10 to 25 
degrees Celsius. The site has bimodal rainfall: short rains (September/November to February) 
and long rains (March to July). 
 
Target Crop and Disease 
Crop: Potato (Solanum tuberosum), variety Shangi. Shangi is the most widely grown variety in 
Kenya; suitable for chips and home consumption; susceptible to late blight; moderately drought 
resistant; yield potential 35 to 40 tonnes per hectare but actual farm yields average 8 tonnes per 
hectare. 
 
Disease: Late blight, caused by the oomycete pathogen Phytophthora infestans. Late blight is 
the most economically significant potato disease globally. It causes annual losses of 
approximately 6.7 to 170 billion USD globally. In Kenya, losses range from 60 to 70%, reaching 
100% under prolonged conducive conditions. The pathogen is transmitted through air, soil, and 
seed tubers. Latently infected seed tubers are a primary inoculum source. The disease causes 
rapid canopy defoliation and tuber infection. 
 
Key Experimental Materials 
Material Details 
Biocontrol Agent Trichoderma asperellum (pure spore powder from Real IPM Kenya). Used at 
33% (3.0 x 10^6 CFU/mL), 66% (7.0 x 10^6 CFU/mL), and 100% (1 x 10^7 
CFU/mL) of Manufacturer Recommended Rate. 
Fungicide 1 Ridomil (Metalaxyl 4% + Mancozeb 64%). Applied at 2.5 g/L. Manufacturer 
Recommended Interval: 7 days. 
Fungicide 2 Mistress 72 (Cynamoxil 4% + Mancozeb 64%). Used at 2 g/L as positive control 
in bioassay and field experiments. 
Seed Material Apical cuttings (tissue culture, 20 cm height) and seed tubers (40-60 g), both 
Shangi variety from KALRO Tigoni. 
Inoculum P. infestans zoospore suspension at 4 x 10^4 zoospores/mL for field inoculation; 
1 x 10^4 zoospores/mL for detached leaf assay. 
 
Kenya Seed System Context 
The formal seed sector supplies less than 5% of certified potato seed required per cropping 
season. The deficit is met by informal systems including farm-saved seed, peer-to-peer 
purchase, and local market purchases. Farm-saved seed is typically latently infected with P. 
infestans, accelerating early epidemic establishment. Seed costs represent up to 42% of total 
potato production costs in Kenya. Tissue culture-derived apical cuttings are an emerging 
technology to address the seed deficit. 
 
 
OBJ1: In Vitro Efficacy Study (AJMR 2020) 
Full citation: Kilonzi J. M., Mafurah J. J., and Nyongesa M. W. (2020). In vitro efficacy of 
Trichoderma asperellum and detached leaflet assay on late blight pathogen: Phytophthora 
infestans. African Journal of Microbiology Research, Vol. 14(5), pp. 148-157. DOI: 
10.5897/AJMR2019.9195. 
 
OBJ1: Study Objectives 
• Determine antifungal activity of T. asperellum against P. infestans in vitro using dual 
culture method. 
• Assess antagonistic effects of T. asperellum on P. infestans using detached leaflet 
bioassay. 
• Evaluate compatibility of T. asperellum with Ridomil and Mistress 72 fungicides. 
 
OBJ1: Methods 
In vitro antifungal bioassay: Dual culture on Potato Dextrose Agar (PDA). P. infestans mycelial 
plug inoculated on PDA, then T. asperellum suspensions added 1 cm from pathogen inoculation 
point. Treatments: T. asperellum at 33%, 66%, 100%; Ridomil (2.5 g/L); Mistress 72 (2 g/L); P. 
infestans only (negative control). Incubation at 18 (+/-2) degrees C, alternating 12h light/12h 
dark for 7 days. Completely randomized design, 3 replications. Inhibition calculated as: I = (R1 - 
R2) / R1 x 100, where R1 = pathogen radius in control, R2 = pathogen radius in treatment. 
 
Detached leaflet assay: Healthy leaflets (6 cm x 4.5 cm) from middle canopy of apical cuttings 
(6-7 weeks old) in glasshouse. Leaflets pre-treated by dipping in T. asperellum suspensions for 
1 second. P. infestans suspension (1 x 10^4 zoospores/mL) applied to abaxial surface. 
Incubation at 20 (+/-2) degrees C. Lesion size measured: S = pi(L + W)^2 / 4. Measurements 
taken on days 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 after inoculation. 
 
Compatibility test: T. asperellum mycelia on PDA exposed to 40 microL of Ridomil (2.5 g/L) and 
Mistress 72 (0.5 g/L). Growth observed for 7 days.

OBJ1: Key Findings 
• T. asperellum at 66% and 100% concentrations both achieved approximately 91% 
mycelial growth inhibition of P. infestans by day 7, not significantly different from each 
other (P = 0.05). 
• T. asperellum at 33% gave only 38% inhibition and was statistically similar to the 
untreated control for lesion size. 
• Ridomil and Mistress 72 achieved 100% inhibition by day 7 in vitro and 0 lesion size in 
detached leaf assay. 
• T. asperellum at 66% produced final lesion size of 1.91 cm2 and 100% produced 1.89 
cm2, not significantly different. 
• T. asperellum at 33% produced lesion size of 3.50 cm2, similar to the untreated P. 
infestans control (3.55 cm2). 
• T. asperellum mycelial growth was NOT inhibited by either Ridomil or Mistress 72, 
confirming compatibility with both fungicides. 
• Mistress 72 showed slightly more suppression of T. asperellum than Ridomil, though not 
statistically significant. 
• T. asperellum acts through competition, mycoparasitism, and release of diffusible 
metabolites (zone of inhibition observed). 
• Concentration is a critical factor: biocontrol must reach sufficient levels to release 
adequate antifungal metabolites. 
 
OBJ1: Mechanism of Action 
At 66% and 100% concentrations, T. asperellum exhibited higher mycelial growth rate (64 mm 
and 65 mm respectively) than P. infestans (42 mm) from day 3, enabling competitive 
displacement. A zone of inhibition was observed between colonies, attributed to diffusible 
metabolites. At 33% concentration, no inhibition zone was observed and P. infestans continued 
to grow. Compatibility with fungicides suggests potential for combined integrated disease 
management. 
 
 
OBJ2: Field Efficacy Study (WJAR 2021) 
Full citation: Kilonzi Jackson Mutuku, Mafurah Juma Joseph, Nyongesa Moses Wabomba, and 
Kibe Antony Mwangi (2021). Efficacy of Trichoderma asperellum Seed Treatment and Ridomil 
Application in Managing Late Blight on Potato. World Journal of Agricultural Research, vol. 9, 
no. 2 (2021): 42-52. DOI: 10.12691/wjar-9-2-1. 
 
OBJ2: Study Objectives 
• Determine the effect of T. asperellum seed treatment concentration on late blight 
severity and yield. 
• Compare Ridomil spray intervals (7, 14, 21 days) in managing late blight. 
• Compare apical cuttings vs. seed tubers for disease susceptibility and yield. 
• Compare pericardial injection vs. dipping as seed treatment methods. 
 
OBJ2: Experimental Design 
Two experiments conducted over short rain season (September 2018 to February 2019) and 
long rain season (March to July 2019). Randomized Complete Block Design in split-split-plot 
arrangement, 3 replications. Main plot: Ridomil spray regime (unsprayed, 7-day, 14-day, 21-day 
intervals). Sub-plot: Planting material (apical cuttings, seed tubers). Sub-sub-plot: Seed 
treatment (untreated, Mistress 72 at 2 g/L, T. asperellum at 33%, 66%, 100%). Plot size: 3 m x 3 
m, spacing 0.75 m x 0.3 m. Path width: 1.5 m between sub-plots, 2 m between main plots. 
 
OBJ2: Weather Conditions 
Short rain season: 21 wet days, warm temperatures (average 24.5 degrees C), low relative 
humidity (64%). Long rain season: 62 wet days, cool temperatures (average 20 degrees C), 
high relative humidity (77%). Late blight developed more rapidly in the long rain season (100% 
disease severity in unprotected plots) compared to short rain season (52%).

Pericardial injection delivered T. asperellum uniformly into tuber tissues without energy cost of 
skin penetration. Dipping provides surface coating that creates a natural barrier against P. 
infestans haustorial penetration. Despite higher yield from injection, dipping is preferred at scale 
due to practicality and cost-effectiveness. 
 
OBJ2: Key Findings 
• T. asperellum at 66% and 100% concentrations reduced disease severity by 36% and 
38% respectively compared to untreated plots, and increased yield by 20% and 21%. 
• T. asperellum at 33% concentration was NOT effective and showed disease levels 
similar to untreated control. 
• Seed treatment with T. asperellum alone (without fungicide) was insufficient to manage 
late blight; crops were completely destroyed prior to tuberization. 
• 7-day and 14-day Ridomil spray intervals were not significantly different in disease 
control or yield. 
• 21-day interval was insufficient for late blight management, especially during prolonged 
wet conditions. 
• Combination of T. asperellum at 66% or 100% + 7- or 14-day Ridomil interval gave 
optimal results. 
• T. asperellum at optimal concentration improved emergence rate: untreated 68%, T. 
asperellum 33% = 79%, T. asperellum 66% = 96%, T. asperellum 100% = 100%. 
• Plants from T. asperellum 66% and 100% remained dark green at harvesting while 
others were yellowish-brown. 
• Seed treatment by dipping is recommended for commercial scale due to practicality; 
automated dipping can address large-scale needs. 
 
 
OBJ3: Cost-Benefit Analysis Study (JAS 2020) 
Full citation: Kilonzi M. Jackson, Mafurah J. Joseph, Nyongesa M. Wambomba, and Ng'ang'a 
Nancy (2020). Cost Benefit Analyses in Managing Late Blight Through Trichoderma asperellum 
Seed Treatment and Ridomil Application on Potato. Journal of Agricultural Science, Vol. 12, No. 
7; 2020. doi:10.5539/jas.v12n7p32. 
 
OBJ3: Study Objectives 
• Determine costs and benefits of T. asperellum seed treatment in combination with 
Ridomil spray regimes. 
• Compare cost-benefit of apical cuttings vs. seed tubers as planting material. 
• Compare cost-benefit of pericardial injection vs. dipping for seed treatment. 
• Determine marginal rate of return (MRR%) for each treatment combination. 
 
OBJ3: Key Disease and Yield Results 
• Long rain season: average temperatures 17-20 degrees C, relative humidity 86% - more 
conducive for P. infestans. Disease severity up to 100% in negative control. Short rain 
season: 19-24.5 degrees C, 65% RH - disease severity up to 54% in negative control. 
• Unsprayed plots had the highest disease score and lowest yield, below the farmers' 
average yield of 8 t/ha. 
• T. asperellum at 66% and 100% reduced disease severity by 26% and 27% respectively. 
• T. asperellum at 66% and 100% increased yield by 30% and 29% over untreated control 
respectively. 
• Strong negative correlation between T. asperellum concentration and RAUDPC: r = 
0.93, R-squared = 0.8665. 
• 14-day and 7-day spray intervals were not significantly different in yield or disease score. 
• Apical cuttings had 7.5% higher disease severity and 0.2% lower yield than seed tubers 
(average over both seasons).

OBJ3: Optimal Combination Conclusion 
The combination of 66% or 100% T. asperellum seed treatment by dipping combined with 
Ridomil at 14-day spray interval provided the highest marginal rate of return and was the most 
economically viable treatment. This combination reduced disease severity, improved yield and 
tuber grade distribution, and reduced fungicide costs by 50% compared to 7-day spray interval. 
 
 
OBJ4: Pesticide Residue Study (IJAAR, Accepted) 
Citation: Kilonzi J., Mafurah J., Nyongesa M., and Oyoo J. Effect of Ridomil Application Regime 
in Late Blight Management on Yield and Pesticide Residue in Potato Tubers. International 
Journal of Applied Agricultural Research (IJAAR). Accepted; payment made; awaiting 
publication. 
 
OBJ4: Study Objectives 
• Determine the effect of Ridomil spray intervals (7, 14, 21 days) on late blight severity 
and yield. 
• Quantify metalaxyl residue levels in potato tubers under different spray regimes. 
• Assess metalaxyl residue in market samples from Limuru (Kiambu County) and 
Wakulima (Nairobi) markets. 
• Compare residue levels against European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) acceptable 
daily limits. 
 
OBJ4: Residue Analysis Method 
Method: Soxhlet extraction. Instrument: Gas Chromatography Mass Spectrometer (GC-MS), 
model HP5771A with NIST library 2008. Metalaxyl standard purity: >99% (from Pest Control 
and Products Board, Kenya). Extraction: 10 g sample in dichloromethane:n-hexane (1:1), dried 
with anhydrous sodium sulphate, Soxhlet extraction with hexane:acetone (1:1) for 16 hours. 
Clean-up using silica column with sodium sulphate, silica oxide, and activated charcoal. Limit of 
Detection (LOD): 0.05 mg/kg. Metalaxyl recovery: 98.8%.

OBJ4: Key Findings on Residues 
• Ridomil applied at 7-day interval (manufacturer recommended interval) resulted in 
metalaxyl residue of 1.69 mg/kg in tubers - more than 21 times the EFSA acceptable 
daily limit of 0.08 mg/kg. 
• Limuru market samples exceeded EFSA limits (0.09 mg/kg), suggesting commercially 
sold potatoes in Kenya may pose health risks. 
• Ridomil at 14-day interval produced residue exactly at the EFSA limit (0.08 mg/kg). 
• Ridomil at 21-day interval and Wakulima market samples were below the limit of 
detection. 
• Metalaxyl is a systemic fungicide; it is taken up into tuber tissues and cannot be 
removed by peeling (unlike mancozeb, which is non-systemic). 
• Short harvest-to-market interval in Kenya means minimal time for metalaxyl breakdown 
before consumption. 
• Farm workers face double exposure risk: dermal/aerosol during mixing and application, 
and dietary through consumption of treated produce. 
• Metalaxyl affects liver functionality; recent research links it to breast cancer progression 
and reproductive, nervous, cardiovascular, and respiratory system effects with chronic 
exposure. 
• Wakulima market (Nairobi) serves potatoes from all counties and Tanzania and had safe 
residue levels, possibly due to longer post-harvest storage or supply chains. 
 
OBJ4: Factors Influencing Metalaxyl Dissipation 
• Time between last fungicide application and harvest: shorter interval = higher residue. 
• Application frequency: higher frequency = more accumulation. 
• Environmental factors: temperature, rainfall, and relative humidity affect degradation. 
• Plant physiology: metabolic pathways include hydrolysis and oxidation of methyl ester 
group. 
• Soil microbial degradation: soil microorganisms can break down metalaxyl but may also 
migrate it to lower soil horizons and groundwater. 
 
 
Cross-Paper Synthesis and Integrated Findings 
Integrated Disease Management Recommendation 
Synthesizing all four papers, the optimal integrated approach for managing potato late blight in 
Kenya's highland conditions is: 
• Seed treatment: Dipping seed tubers in T. asperellum at 66% concentration (7.0 x 10^6 
CFU/mL) before planting. 
• Spray regime: Ridomil (Metalaxyl 4% + Mancozeb 64%) applied at 14-day intervals (not 
the manufacturer-recommended 7 days). 
• Rationale: The 14-day combination achieves statistically equivalent disease control and 
yield to the 7-day regime, reduces fungicide cost by 50%, and keeps metalaxyl residue 
at (not above) acceptable limits. 
• Avoiding 33% T. asperellum: This concentration showed no significant difference from 
untreated controls in disease or yield. 
• Avoiding reliance on biocontrol alone: Seed treatment without fungicide was insufficient; 
crops were destroyed before tuberization.

Concentration Threshold 
A clear and consistent concentration threshold exists across both in vitro (OBJ1) and field 
(OBJ2, OBJ3) studies. T. asperellum below 66% (i.e., at 33% = 3.0 x 10^6 CFU/mL) is 
insufficient to suppress P. infestans. At and above 66% (7.0 x 10^6 CFU/mL), effective 
suppression is achieved. 100% (1 x 10^7 CFU/mL) provided marginally higher effectiveness in 
prolonged wet conditions (long rain season) but not statistically different from 66%. 
 
Fungicide Residue Safety Implication 
OBJ4 reveals a public health conflict with the manufacturer-recommended 7-day spray interval: 
residue at 1.69 mg/kg is 21 times the EFSA acceptable daily limit. OBJ2 and OBJ3 
independently demonstrate that the 14-day interval is equally effective agronomically. Together, 
these four papers provide a complete evidence base for recommending a shift from 7-day to 14-
day spray intervals combined with T. asperellum seed treatment, achieving equal or better 
yields, lower costs, and safer residue levels. 
 
 
Glossary of Key Terms 
Term Definition 
AUDPC Area Under Disease Progress Curve. Summarizes disease severity over time. 
Higher value = more disease. 
RAUDPC Relative AUDPC. AUDPC standardized to season length to allow seasonal 
comparison. 
CFU/mL Colony Forming Units per millilitre. Measure of viable microbial concentration. 
MRR% Marginal Rate of Return percentage. Ratio of additional income to additional 
cost, expressed as percentage. Calculated as: (Change in Net Benefits / 
Change in Variable Costs) x 100. 
TVC Total Variable Costs. Costs that vary between treatments used in partial budget 
analysis. 
MRR (Manufacturer 
Recommended 
Rate) 
The concentration of biocontrol agent as recommended by manufacturer (100% 
= MRR). 
Term Definition 
Pericardial / 
Peridermal 
Injection 
Injection of treatment through the skin (periderm) of a seed tuber using 
hypodermic needle. 
DAE Days After Emergence. 
T. asperellum Trichoderma asperellum. A fast-growing beneficial fungus used as biocontrol 
agent. 
P. infestans Phytophthora infestans. The oomycete pathogen causing potato late blight. 
KALRO Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization. Government research 
body. 
LOD Limit of Detection. Minimum detectable concentration; set at 0.05 mg/kg for 
metalaxyl in this study. 
GC-MS Gas Chromatography Mass Spectrometry. Analytical technique for identifying 
and quantifying chemical compounds. 
IDM Integrated Disease Management. Combining multiple approaches (biological, 
chemical, cultural) for disease control. 
EFSA European Food Safety Authority. Sets maximum residue limits used as 
benchmarks in this study. 
Kes / KES Kenyan Shillings. Currency used for economic analysis. 
Apical cuttings Rooted cuttings produced from potato plantlets through tissue culture; disease-
free seed material. 
Ware grade Marketable tubers greater than 60 g (or >60 mm depending on grading system 
used). 
Chatt grade Small unmarketable tubers below 40 g or 25 mm. Higher proportion indicates 
disease damage. 
Seed grade Tubers of 40-60 g (or 25-60 mm). Suitable for planting as seed tubers. 
 
 
Quick Reference Facts for RAG Retrieval 
This section contains discrete factual statements for high-precision retrieval: 
 
• T. asperellum at 66% inhibited P. infestans mycelial growth by 91.10% in vitro; at 100%, 
inhibition was 91.30%. Not significantly different. 
• T. asperellum at 33% inhibited P. infestans by only 38.0% in vitro - ineffective. 
• Ridomil and Mistress 72 achieved 100% inhibition of P. infestans in vitro by day 7. 
• T. asperellum at 66% produced late blight lesion size of 1.91 cm2 on detached leaves at 
day 11; 100% produced 1.89 cm2. 
• T. asperellum 33% and untreated controls produced lesion sizes of 3.50 and 3.55 cm2 
respectively - not significantly different. 
• Ridomil and Mistress 72 had no significant effect on T. asperellum mycelial growth - 
confirming compatibility. 
• In field trials, T. asperellum 66% and 100% reduced disease severity by 36-38% and 
increased yield by 20-21% vs. untreated. 
• 14-day and 7-day Ridomil spray intervals produce statistically equivalent disease control 
and yield in all studies. 
• Metalaxyl residue at 7-day spray interval: 1.69 mg/kg (21x above EFSA limit of 0.08 
mg/kg). 
• Metalaxyl residue at 14-day spray interval: 0.08 mg/kg (exactly at EFSA acceptable 
limit). 
• Metalaxyl residue at 21-day interval and in unsprayed plots: below limit of detection (< 
0.05 mg/kg). 
• Limuru market potato samples contained 0.09 mg/kg metalaxyl - above EFSA limit. 
• Wakulima market (Nairobi) samples had metalaxyl below detection limit - safe. 
• Seed dipping has a cost-benefit ratio 408% higher than pericardial injection for T. 
asperellum application. 
• Dipping seed treatment labour: 11.25 man-days per hectare. Pericardial injection: 90 
man-days per hectare. 
• Apical cutting seed cost (KES 444,440/ha) is 80% higher than seed tuber cost (KES 
135,000/ha). 
• Apical cutting planting requires 114 man-hours per hectare vs. 45 man-hours for seed 
tubers. 
• Apical cuttings result in net loss in both short and long rain seasons when used without 
recycling. 
• Seed tuber net benefit/TVC ratios: 1.06 (short rain) and 0.72 (long rain). 
• Ridomil at 14-day interval saves KES 30,000/ha in fungicide cost and KES 6,400/ha in 
labour vs. 7-day interval. 
• Best MRR% overall: 14-day interval + 66% T. asperellum at 1,963% (short rain) and 
1,191% (long rain). 
• Correlation between T. asperellum concentration and RAUDPC: r = 0.93, R-squared = 
0.8665 (strong negative). 
• Kenya's formal seed system supplies less than 5% of required potato seed; deficit filled 
by informal sector. 
• Late blight annual economic losses: 170 billion USD globally; 60-70% yield loss in Kenya 
under conducive conditions. 
• Farmers' average potato yield in Kenya: 8 t/ha; potential yield: 40 t/ha. 
• Shangi variety: susceptible to late blight, suitable for chips and home consumption, most 
widely grown in Kenya. 
• Pericardial injection produced 7.73-8.3% higher yield than dipping despite higher 
disease score. 
• Unprotected potato crops during long rain season suffered up to 100% defoliation; yield 
below 1 t/ha. 
• EFSA metalaxyl acceptable daily intake: 0.08 mg/kg body weight per day (EC Directive 
91/414/EEC).
